verses.zh: 尼布甲尼撒王造了一个金像，高六十肘，宽六肘，立在巴比伦省杜拉平原。
verses.en: [NOTE:1] King Nebuchadnezzar had a golden[NOTE:2] statue made.[NOTE:3] It was 90 feet[NOTE:4] tall and 9 feet[NOTE:5] wide. He erected it on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.
notes: The LXX introduces this chapter with the following chronological note: “in the eighteenth year of.” Such a date would place these events at about the time of the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 b.c. (cf. 2 Kgs 25:8). However, there seems to be no real basis for associating the events of Daniel 3 with this date.

There is no need to think of Nebuchadnezzar’s image as being solid gold. No doubt the sense is that it was overlaid with gold (cf. Isa 40:19; Jer 10:3-4), with the result that it presented a dazzling self-compliment to the greatness of Nebuchadnezzar’s achievements.
According to a number of patristic authors, the image represented a deification of Nebuchadnezzar himself. This is not clear from the biblical text, however.
Aram “60 cubits.” Assuming a length of 18 inches for the standard cubit, the image would be 90 feet (27.4 m) high.

Aram “6 cubits.” Assuming a length of 18 inches for the standard cubit, the image would be 9 feet (2.74 m) wide.sn The dimensions of the image (90 feet high and 9 feet wide) imply that it did not possess normal human proportions, unless a base for the image is included in the height dimension. The ancient world knew of other tall statues. For example, the Colossus of Rhodes—the huge statue of Helios which stood (ca. 280-224 b.c.) at the entrance to the harbor at Rhodes and was one of the seven wonders of the ancient world—was said to be 70 cubits (105 ft or 32 m) in height, which would make it even taller than Nebuchadnezzar’s image.
verses.commentary:
3:1 The LXX has an added phrase which dates this event as "in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar," which would be
587 B.C. This is one of the dates for exiles being taken from Jerusalaem and the destruction of the city and the temple.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

▣ "an image of gold" The image (BDB 1109 ‒ statue, form) may have been similar to the
vision of a human person made of four metals from chapter 2. It is either

- an elongated human form

- a tall obelisk of uncertain shape

The Aramaic term can mean "obelisk." The normal physical proportions of the human body is five
to one, but the image's height and width would be ten to one. A large platform has been found six miles
from the ruins of the ancient city of Babylon, which measures forty-five feet by forty-five feet by eighteen
feet. This could have been the base of this image.

▣ "of gold" This seems to mean overlaid with gold and we have biblical and secular examples of this, such as

- Aaron's golden calf (Exod. 32)

- Isaiah 40:19; 41:7; 44:10

- Jeremiah 10:4,14

- Herodotus 1.183

▣ "sixty cubits and its width was six cubits" This would make the image about ninety
feet tall by nine feet wide if we base our measurements on a cubit (BDB 1081) as being eighteen inches,
which denotes the distance from the longest finger to the elbow of a normal sized human being of that
period. The Colossus of Rhodes was seventy cubits high (i.e., 105 feet), so this was not out of the realm
of ancient technology. See IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 735.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CUBIT

▣ "the plain of Dura" The term (BDB 1087) seems to come from the "duru" which means "an
enclosing wall" or "fortress" (Akkadian). We have found several documents from Babylon which mention
the Plain of Dura. However, its exact location is uncertain. With the finding of the large base several
miles from the city of Babylon, this is a possibility.

verses.zh: 尼布甲尼撒王差人将总督、钦差、巡抚、臬司、藩司、谋士、法官，和各省的官员都召了来，为尼布甲尼撒王所立的像行开光之礼。
verses.en: Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent out a summons to assemble the satraps, prefects, governors, counselors, treasurers, judges, magistrates,[NOTE:1] and all the other authorities of the province to attend the dedication of the statue that he[NOTE:2] had erected.
notes: The specific duties of the seven types of officials listed here (cf. vv. 3, 27) are unclear. The Aramaic words that are used are transliterations of Akkadian or Persian technical terms whose exact meanings are uncertain. The translations given here follow suggestions set forth in BDB.
Aram “Nebuchadnezzar the king.” The proper name and title have been replaced by the relative pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
verses.commentary:
3:2-3,5 These eight categories of governmental officials come from Persian words (NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 604). However,
this by itself, does not necessitate a later date for the composition of Daniel. It is probable that the writings of Daniel were edited
and compiled after his death in the Persian period (i.e., Cyrus II).

Loan words by themselves do not indicate the original date of the writing.

- loan words common in ANE

- later Jewish compilers update the terminology

SPECIAL TOPIC: SCRIBES

3:2 "the king sent word to assemble" We have, from Sargon II's records, examples of this
same type of royal assembly, possibly an annual "loyalty oath."

verses.zh: 于是总督、钦差、巡抚、臬司、藩司、谋士、法官，和各省的官员都聚集了来，要为尼布甲尼撒王所立的像行开光之礼，就站在尼布甲尼撒所立的像前。
verses.en: So the satraps, prefects, governors, counselors, treasurers, judges, magistrates, and all the other provincial authorities assembled for the dedication of the statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had erected. They were standing in front of the statue that Nebuchadnezzar had erected.[NOTE:1]
notes: The LXX and Theodotion lack the words “that Nebuchadnezzar had erected.”
verses.commentary:
3:3 The repetitive nature of this chapter, both in the listing of the government officials and
the musical instruments, is characteristic of

- Hebraic writing

- obelistic writing

▣ "satraps" This Aramaic governmental term (BDB 1080) reflects a Median word which means
"protector of the land." In the later Persian Empire it referred to the twenty governors (Herodotus)
of the provinces (cf. Ezra 8:36; Esther 3:12; 8:9; 9:3), but its exact meaning in the earlier
neo-Babylonian Empire is uncertain, possibly "prince" (cf. TEV).

▣ "prefects" The meaning of this Aramaic governmental term (BDB 1104) is uncertain, possibly
an Akkadian term for those who report directly to the satraps. Daniel was appointed to this position
over all the wise men of Babylon in Dan. 2:48.

▣ "governors" The meaning of this Aramaic governmental term (BDB 1108) is also uncertain. The
related Hebrew term denotes "governors" (cf. 1 Kgs. 10:15; 20:24; 2 Kgs. 18:24; often in Ezra, Nehemiah,
and Esther; Isa. 36:9; Jer. 51:23,28,57; and several times in the post-exilic prophets).

▣ "counselors" This is another Aramaic governmental term (BDB 1078) of uncertain meaning. The
typical translation is "counselor," but some scholars think it refers to

- a military position (BDB 1078)

- "treasurers" (cf. Ezra 7:21)

▣ "magistrates" This Aramaic governmental term (BDB 1118) is also uncertain. William Holladay,
A Concise Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, says it refers to a police official
(p. 425) from a Persian loan word.

▣ "the rulers of the provinces" This refers to lesser governmental officials (BDB 1097). This
event was a gathering of all governmental workers of all levels (cf. Dan. 3:4,7).

verses.zh: 那时传令的大声呼叫说：「各方、各国、各族（原文是舌：下同）的人哪，有令传与你们：
verses.en: Then the herald[NOTE:1] made a loud[NOTE:2] proclamation: “To you, O peoples, nations, and language groups, the following command is given:[NOTE:3]
notes: According to BDB 1097 s.v. כָּרוֹז the Aramaic word used here is a Greek loanword, but other scholars have argued instead for a Persian derivation (HALOT 1902 s.v. *כָּרוֹז).
Aram “in strength.”
Aram “they are saying.”
verses.commentary:
3:4-7 The call for "all" the peoples to bow down and worship the image must be an example of "representative
government." All the peoples" (i.e., languages, nations) were not on the Plain of Dura that day, but their appointed
governmental leaders were. This is similar "representative government" to Exod. 19:7, where Moses called the tribal
leaders to ratify the covenant of YHWH.

verses.zh: 你们一听见角、笛、琵琶、琴、瑟、笙，和各样乐器的声音，就当俯伏敬拜尼布甲尼撒王所立的金像。
verses.en: When you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither,[NOTE:1] trigon, harp, pipes, and all kinds of music, you must[NOTE:2] bow down and pay homage to the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar has erected.
notes: The word zither (Aramaic קִיתָרוֹס [qitaros]), and the words for harp (Aramaic פְּסַנְתֵּרִין [pesanterin]) and pipes (Aramaic סוּמְפֹּנְיָה [sumponeyah]), are of Greek derivation. Though much has been made of this in terms of suggesting a date in the Hellenistic period for the writing of the book, it is not surprising that a few Greek cultural terms, all of them the names of musical instruments, should appear in this book. As a number of scholars have pointed out, the bigger surprise (if, in fact, the book is to be dated to the Hellenistic period) may be that there are so few Greek loanwords in Daniel.
The imperfect Aramaic verbs have here an injunctive nuance.
verses.commentary:
3:5,7,10 "at the moment you hear the sound of" This list of musical instruments refers to the
Babylonian national orchestra. This may have been the Babylonian national anthem (cf. Dan. 3:10). We have
a record from Babylonian documents of a similar party where 150 musicians played. It is obvious that
the neo-Babylonians enjoyed music and included it in all of their festive occasions.

3:5

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NJB, JPS, NIV, NEB, LXX
"horn"

Peshitta
"trumpet"

In Daniel 7:7-8,11,20,21,24 this Aramaic word (BDB 1111) refers to an animal horn. Here,
it refers to a musical instrument, possibly made from an animal horn.

▣

NASB, NKJV, NIV, Peshitta
"flute"

NRSV, NJB, JPS, NEB, LXX
"pipe"

The Aramaic term (BDB 1117) refers to some type of wind instrument.

▣

NASB, NRSV, NJB, LXX
"lyre"

NKJV, Peshitta
"harp"

JPS, NIV, NEB
"zither"

This is a Greek loan word (kitharis), which denotes a stringed instrument
(harp, BDB 1111).

▣

NASB, NRSV, LXX
"trigon"

NJB
"zither"

JPS, NIV, NEB
"triangle"

Peshitta
sackbut"

This reflects another Greek loan word (sambukē), which denotes a stringed
instrument with four strings (BDB 1113).

▣

NASB, JPS, Peshitta
"psaltery"

NRSV, NJB, NIV, LXX
"harp"

NEB
"dulcimer"

This (BDB 1108) denotes a triangular shaped stringed instrument with a sounding board
(William Holladay, A Concise Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, p. 418).

▣

NASB, NJB
"bagpipe"

NRSV
"drum"

NEB
"music"

LXX
"a symphony of all kinds of musical instruments"

Peshitta
"all kinds of music"

There is confusion in the English translation as to how many musical instruments are
listed. The Masoretic Text and the Septuagint have only five in Dan. 3:7, but this sixth one is listed
in Dan. 3:5 and 10. It may refer to a double pipe similar to a Pan flute (BDB 1104).

It is also possible that this last term means "in unison" (cf. NKJV, TEV, LXX, Peshitta).

▣ "fall down and worship" Both VERBS are Peal IMPERFECT
(BDB 1103 and 1104). This shows the religious and political significance of this human image (cf. Dan. 3:12). This
is the reason that the three Hebrew children refused to participate. It is uncertain if the Neo-Babylonian
rulers claimed deity (the image as a representative of Nebuchadnezzar, cf. Dan. 2:38), as did the Pharaohs
of Egypt and some later Caesars of Rome.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORSHIP

verses.zh: 凡不俯伏敬拜的，必立时扔在烈火的窑中。」
verses.en: Whoever does not bow down and pay homage will immediately[NOTE:1] be thrown into the midst of a furnace of blazing fire!”
notes: Aram “in that hour.”
verses.commentary:
3:6,15 "immediately" Literally this is "same hour" (BDB 1116, cf. Dan. 4:30; 5:5; see note at Roland deVaux,
Ancient Israel, vol. 1, p. 183). This is the first use of the term
"hour" in the OT. There is some discussion if the term and concept began with the Babylonians or the Greeks.
We must remember that this does not refer to our precise sixty minutes because they were using more crude
timing instruments.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOUR

▣ "cast into the midst of a furnace of blazing fire" Because of the description found in
Daniel 3 and also because of archaeology discoveries, it seems that this was a large, domed kiln with an
opening at the top and an earthen ramp leading up to it. It also had a door on the bottom for putting
in charcoal and taking out ashes.

This was a common form of capital punishment during this period
(cf. Code of Hammurabi 110,157 and Jer. 29:22).

verses.zh: 因此各方、各国、各族的人民一听见角、笛、琵琶、琴、瑟，和各样乐器的声音，就都俯伏敬拜尼布甲尼撒王所立的金像。
verses.en: Therefore when they all[NOTE:1] heard the sound of the horn, flute, zither, trigon, harp, pipes,[NOTE:2] and all kinds of music, all the peoples, nations, and language groups began bowing down and paying homage to the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had erected.
notes: Aram “all the peoples.”
Though not in the Aramaic text of BHS, this word appears in many medieval Hebrew MSS, some LXX MSS, and the Vulgate (cf. vv. 5, 10, 15).

verses.zh: 那时，有几个迦勒底人进前来控告犹大人。
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] at that time certain[NOTE:2] Chaldeans came forward and brought malicious accusations against[NOTE:3] the Jews.
notes: This expression is absent in Theodotion.
Aram “men.”
Aram “ate the pieces of.” This is a rather vivid idiom for slander.
verses.commentary:
3:8 "certain Chaldeans" It must be remembered that "Chaldeans" can be

- a racial group of the southern Tigris-Euphrates River Valley (cf. Dan. 5:30)

- a group of wise men and priests (cf. Dan. 2:2,4,5,10; 3:8; 4:7; 5:7,11)

In this context, #2 makes more sense. Remember, words have meaning only in sentences and sentences have
meaning only in paragraphs.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

▣ "brought charges against the Jews" This is literally "chewed up the pieces of"
(cf. Dan. 6:25, NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p.396, #5). This is a very strong phrase (BDB 1080, Peal PERFECT and BDB 1111)
which shows the vehemence of the charges. From the text it is obvious that there was jealousy involved
because these Jewish young men had been assigned a place of leadership (cf. Dan. 3:12; 6:4). Also, there was an ethnic
prejudice because of the mention of their origin (cf. Dan. 3:12).

For "Jews" (BDB 1095) see
SPECIAL TOPIC: JEWS

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW PEOPLE

verses.zh: 他们对尼布甲尼撒王说：「愿王万岁！
verses.en: They said[NOTE:1] to King Nebuchadnezzar, “O king, live forever![NOTE:2]
notes: Aram “answered and said,” a common Aramaic idiom that occurs repeatedly in this chapter.

O king, live forever! is a comment of typical court courtesy that is not necessarily indicative of the real sentiments of the speaker. Ancient oriental court protocol could sometimes require a certain amount of hypocrisy.
verses.commentary:
3:9 "O king, live forever" See note at Dan. 2:4 and
SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('OLAM)

verses.zh: 王啊，你曾降旨说，凡听见角、笛、琵琶、琴、瑟、笙，和各样乐器声音的都当俯伏敬拜金像。
verses.en: You have issued an edict, O king, that everyone must bow down and pay homage to the golden statue when they hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, trigon, harp, pipes, and all kinds of music.

verses.zh: 凡不俯伏敬拜的，必扔在烈火的窑中。
verses.en: And whoever does not bow down and pay homage must be thrown into the midst of a furnace of blazing fire.

verses.zh: 现在有几个犹大人，就是王所派管理巴比伦省事务的沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌；王啊，这些人不理你，不事奉你的神，也不敬拜你所立的金像。」
verses.en: But there are Jewish men whom you appointed over the administration of the province of Babylon—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—and these men[NOTE:1] have not shown proper respect to you, O king. They don’t serve your gods, and they don’t pay homage to the golden statue that you have erected.”
notes: Daniel’s absence from this scene has sparked the imagination of commentators, some of whom have suggested that perhaps he was unable to attend the dedication due to sickness or absence prompted by business. Hippolytus supposed that Daniel may have been watching from a distance.
verses.commentary:
3:12 "namely, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego" It is uncertain where Daniel was at this
time. It could be that he was sick or on a governmental assignment. This would be unusual because all
the other government officials were present.

For a summary of the possibilities related to Daniel's absence see The Expositor's Bible
Commentary, vol. 7, pp. 55-56.

For the Babylonian meaning of these names, see Dan. 1:7.

▣ "have disregarded you; they do not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have
set up" Imagine the peer pressure that there must have been on these young men who were so far from
home and who were placed in such important places of leadership.

Nebuchadnezzar II must have forgotten his praise of YHWH from Dan. 2:46-47.

verses.zh: 当时，尼布甲尼撒冲冲大怒，吩咐人把沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌带过来，他们就把那些人带到王面前。
verses.en: Then Nebuchadnezzar in a fit of rage[NOTE:1] demanded that they bring[NOTE:2] Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego before him. So they brought them[NOTE:3] before the king.
notes: Aram “in anger and wrath”; NASB “in rage and anger.” The expression is a hendiadys.
The Aramaic infinitive is active.
Aram “these men.” The pronoun is used in the translation to avoid undue repetition.
verses.commentary:
3:13 "in rage and anger" Nebuchadnezzar II was prone to anger (cf. Dan. 2:12; 3:19). Oriental kings
were not accustomed to people disobeying their orders!

This phrase (BDB 1112 and 1095) is called a hendiadys, which is characteristic of Daniel
writing style. See note at Dan. 2:12. The king was so angry that he physically shook!

verses.zh: 尼布甲尼撒问他们说：「沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌，你们不事奉我的神，也不敬拜我所立的金像，是故意的吗？
verses.en: Nebuchadnezzar said to them, “Is it true, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that you don’t serve my gods and that you don’t pay homage to the golden statue that I erected?
verses.commentary:
3:14 Nebuchadnezzar II tries to give them a second chance (cf. Dan. 3:15, they were excellent
administrators), but their refusal just proves to intensify his anger. He took their rejection of his
gods as a personal rejection.

verses.zh: 你们再听见角、笛、琵琶、琴、瑟、笙，和各样乐器的声音，若俯伏敬拜我所造的像，却还可以；若不敬拜，必立时扔在烈火的窑中，有何神能救你们脱离我手呢？」
verses.en: Now if you are ready, when you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, trigon, harp, pipes, and all kinds of music, you must bow down and pay homage to the statue that I had made. If you don’t pay homage to it, you will immediately be thrown into the midst of the furnace of blazing fire. Now, who is that god who can rescue you from my power?”[NOTE:1]
notes: Aram “hand,” as also in v. 17.
verses.commentary:
3:15 "what god is there who can deliver you out of my hands" This is theologically similar to
2 Kgs. 18:33 and 19:12. YHWH is openly challenged to demonstrate His existence, power, and compassion
to those who trust Him (cf. Dan. 3:28). YHWH reveals Himself to the nations by showing His sovereignty
and love for His covenant people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

verses.zh: 沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌对王说：「尼布甲尼撒啊，这件事我们不必回答你；
verses.en: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego replied to King Nebuchadnezzar,[NOTE:1] “We do not need to give you a reply[NOTE:2] concerning this.
notes: In the MT this word is understood to begin the following address (“answered and said to the king, ‘O Nebuchadnezzar’”). However, it seems unlikely that Nebuchadnezzar’s subordinates would address the king in such a familiar way, particularly in light of the danger that they now found themselves in. The present translation implies moving the verse-dividing atnakh from “king” to “Nebuchadnezzar.”
Aram “to return a word to you.”

verses.zh: 即便如此，我们所事奉的　神能将我们从烈火的窑中救出来。王啊，他也必救我们脱离你的手；
verses.en: If[NOTE:1] our God whom we are serving exists,[NOTE:2] he is able to rescue us from the furnace of blazing fire, and he will rescue us, O king, from your power as well.
notes: The ancient versions typically avoid the conditional element of v. 17.

The Aramaic expression used here is very difficult to interpret. The question concerns the meaning and syntax of אִיתַי (ʾitay, “is” or “exist”). There are several possibilities. (1) Some interpreters take this word closely with the participle later in the verse יָכִל (yakhil, “able”), understanding the two words to form a periphrastic construction (“if our God is…able”; cf. H. Bauer and P. Leander, Grammatik des Biblisch-Aramäischen, 365, §111b). But the separation of the two elements from one another is not an argument in favor of this understanding. (2) Other interpreters take the first part of v. 17 to mean “If it is so, then our God will deliver us” (cf. KJV, ASV, RSV, NASB). However, the normal sense of ʾitay is existence; on this point see F. Rosenthal, Grammar, 41, §95. The present translation maintains the sense of existence for the verb (“If our God…exists”), even though the statement is admittedly difficult to understand in this light. The statement may be an implicit reference back to Nebuchadnezzar’s comment in v. 15, which denies the existence of a god capable of delivering from the king’s power, thus their statement is rhetorically adapted to the perspective of the person they are addressing.
verses.commentary:
3:17 "If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the furnace of blazing fire"
Nebuchadnezzar II had made this a contest between the gods of Babylon and the God of Judah by asserting
that no one could deliver them out of his hand (cf. Dan. 3:15). The descriptive title, "the God who is
able," is also in Dan. 3:29 and in the NT at Rom. 16:25; Eph. 3:20; Jude 24.

The NET Bible translates this phrase as "If our God whom we are serving exists, he is able
to rescue us from the furnace of blazing fire." The Anchor Bible, vol. 23, also has a translation that
tries to employ the Aramaic word "exist" (BDB 1095, KB 410 [Hebrew root]) — "If there is a God able to save us, such as our God, he
will save us from the white-hot furnace" (p. 155).

SPECIAL TOPIC: DESCRIPTIVE TITLES FOR GOD

verses.zh: 即或不然，王啊，你当知道我们决不事奉你的神，也不敬拜你所立的金像。」
verses.en: But if he does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we don’t serve your gods, and we will not pay homage to the golden statue that you have erected.”
verses.commentary:
3:18 "But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king that we are not going
to serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up" They believed that God was able,
but they were not being presumptuous by demanding a miracle. They had faith in God, not in circumstances (i.e., Job 13:15).

verses.zh: 当时，尼布甲尼撒怒气填胸，向沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌变了脸色，吩咐人把窑烧热，比寻常更加七倍；
verses.en: Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with rage, and his disposition changed[NOTE:1] toward Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He gave orders[NOTE:2] to heat the furnace seven times hotter than it was normally heated.
notes: Aram “the appearance of his face was altered”; cf. NLT “his face became distorted with rage”; NAB “[his] face became livid with utter rage.”
Aram “he answered and said.”
verses.commentary:
3:19 "seven times more than it was usually heated" This is an obvious use of figurative language
(cf. v. 22). It simply means that the brick kiln was heated as hot as it possibly could be heated. The hyperbole reflects Nebuchadnezzar II's anger!

SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #4

verses.zh: 又吩咐他军中的几个壮士，将沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌捆起来，扔在烈火的窑中。
verses.en: He ordered strong[NOTE:1] soldiers in his army to tie up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and to throw them into the furnace of blazing fire.
notes: This is sometimes taken as a comparative: “[some of the] strongest.”
verses.commentary:
3:20

NASB
"valiant warriors"

NKJV
"mighty men"

NRSV
"some of the strongest guards"

TEV, REB. JPSOA
"the strongest men"

NJB
"certain stalwarts from his army"

The CONSTRUCT (BDB 1086 and 1093) implies his strongest military guards.
Nebuchadnezzar's anger will result in the death of these valued servants (cf. Dan. 3:22).

verses.zh: 这三人穿着裤子、内袍、外衣，和别的衣服，被捆起来扔在烈火的窑中。
verses.en: So those men were tied up while still wearing their cloaks, trousers, turbans, and other clothes,[NOTE:1] and were thrown into the furnace[NOTE:2] of blazing fire.
notes: There is a great deal of uncertainty with regard to the specific nature of these items of clothing.
Aram “into the midst of the furnace.” For stylistic reasons the words “the midst of” have been left untranslated.
verses.commentary:
3:21 "their trousers, their coats, their caps, and their other clothes" This was their official
attire showing the high governmental level they had attained in the neo-Babylonian empire.

verses.zh: 因为王命紧急，窑又甚热，那抬沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌的人都被火焰烧死。
verses.en: But since the king’s command was so urgent, and the furnace was so excessively hot, the men who escorted[NOTE:1] Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were killed[NOTE:2] by the leaping flames.[NOTE:3]
notes: Aram “caused to go up.”
The Aramaic verb is active.
Aram “the flame of the fire” (so KJV, ASV, NASB); NRSV “the raging flames.”
verses.commentary:
3:22 "the furnace had been made extremely hot, the flame of the fire slew those men" This is a graphic
detail of the extreme heat into which the three Hebrew boys were thrown. The fall itself should have killed
them, much less the temperature.

verses.zh: 沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌这三个人都被捆着落在烈火的窑中。
verses.en: But those three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, fell into the furnace[NOTE:1] of blazing fire while still securely bound.[NOTE:2]
notes: Aram “into the midst of the furnace.” For stylistic reasons the words “the midst of” have been left untranslated.

The deuterocanonical writings known as The Prayer of Azariah and The Song of the Three present at this point a confession and petition for God’s forgiveness and a celebration of God’s grace for the three Jewish youths in the fiery furnace. Though not found in the Hebrew/Aramaic text of Daniel, these compositions do appear in the ancient Greek versions.
verses.commentary:
3:23 After this verse is the place where the Septuagint inserts two Apocryphal writings, "The Song
of the Three Youths" and "The Prayer of Assariah." These two Apocryphal writings assert that the dew of
heaven brought by the angel of the Lord kept the Hebrew youths from death.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

verses.zh: 那时，尼布甲尼撒王惊奇，急忙起来，对谋士说：「我捆起来扔在火里的不是三个人吗？」他们回答王说：「王啊，是。」
verses.en: Then King Nebuchadnezzar was startled and quickly got up. He said to his ministers, “Wasn’t it three men that we tied up and threw[NOTE:1] into[NOTE:2] the fire?” They replied to the king, “For sure, O king.”
notes: Aram “we threw…bound.”
Aram “into the midst of.”
verses.commentary:
3:24 Notice that Nebuchadnezzar, talking to his counselors, says, "did not we
cast?" He wants to spread the blame.

verses.zh: 王说：「看哪，我见有四个人，并没有捆绑，在火中游行，也没有受伤；那第四个的相貌好像神子。」
verses.en: He answered, “But I see four men, untied and walking around in the midst of the fire! No harm has come to them! And the appearance of the fourth is like that of a god!”[NOTE:1]
notes: The phrase like that of a god is in Aramaic “like that of a son of the gods.” Many patristic writers understood this phrase in a christological sense (i.e., “the Son of God”). But it should be remembered that these are words spoken by a pagan who is seeking to explain things from his own polytheistic frame of reference; for him the phrase “like a son of the gods” is equivalent to “like a divine being.” Despite the king’s description though, the fourth person probably was an angel who had come to deliver the three men, or was a theophany.
verses.commentary:
3:25 "I see four men loosed and walking about in the midst of the fire" There has
been much discussion about how Nebuchadnezzar II could see these men. It seems that the brick kiln was a domed
structure with a place at the bottom for the removal of ashes. Apparently, he looked through the hole
in the bottom and saw the young men walking about.

▣ "the fourth is like a son of the gods" This is simply polytheistic jargon for a supernatural being. A considerable
amount of speculation has been made about this fourth personage. He is an angel of the Lord
(cf. Dan. 3:28 also 6:22). It is humorous to note that when Nebuchadnezzar II calls the boys out by name, he makes no mention of that fourth person!

SPECIAL TOPIC: sons of. . .

SPECIAL TOPIC: The Angel of the Lord

verses.zh: 于是，尼布甲尼撒就近烈火窑门，说：「至高　神的仆人沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌出来，上这里来吧！」沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌就从火中出来了。
verses.en: Then Nebuchadnezzar approached the door of the furnace of blazing fire. He called out,[NOTE:1] “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the most high God, come out! Come here!” Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego emerged from the fire.[NOTE:2]
notes: Aram “answered and said.”
Aram “from the midst of the fire.” For stylistic reasons the words “the midst of” have been left untranslated.

verses.zh: 那些总督、钦差、巡抚，和王的谋士一同聚集看这三个人，见火无力伤他们的身体，头发也没有烧焦，衣裳也没有变色，并没有火燎的气味。
verses.en: Once the satraps, prefects, governors, and ministers of the king had gathered around, they saw that those men were physically[NOTE:1] unharmed by the fire.[NOTE:2] The hair of their heads was not singed, nor were their trousers damaged. Not even the smell of fire was to be found on them!
notes: Aram “in their bodies.”
Aram “the fire did not have power.”
verses.commentary:
3:27 In the presence of all his civil, military, and police officials Nebuchadnezzar is forced
to acknowledge the God of Judah (cf. Dan. 3:28-29) for the second time (i.e., Dan. 2:46-49).

This striking evidence of God's protection is similar to Isa. 43:2 which used water and fire imagery. In Isaiah
it is imagery for earthly struggles and persecution, but in Daniel it is literal (cf. Heb. 11:34).

verses.zh: 尼布甲尼撒说：「沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌的　神是应当称颂的！他差遣使者救护倚靠他的仆人，他们不遵王命，舍去己身，在他们　神以外不肯事奉敬拜别神。
verses.en: Nebuchadnezzar exclaimed,[NOTE:1] “Praised be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent forth his angel[NOTE:2] and has rescued his servants who trusted in him, ignoring[NOTE:3] the edict of the king and giving up their bodies rather than[NOTE:4] serve or pay homage to any god other than their God!
notes: Aram “answered and said.”

The king identifies the “son of the gods” (v. 25) as an angel. Comparable Hebrew expressions are used elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible for the members of God’s angelic assembly (see Gen 6:2, 4; Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7; Pss 29:1; 89:6). An angel later comes to rescue Daniel from the lions (Dan 6:22).
Aram “they changed” or “violated.”
Aram “so that they might not.”
verses.commentary:
3:28-29 This statement is very similar to Dan. 2:46-48. It is an outburst of a fearful polytheist
in the face of the power of YHWH. It is not Nebuchadnezzar's confession of faith.

3:28 "who put their trust in Him" Not only is the One True God emphasized, but also the need
for personal, active trust in Him (BDB 1113, Hithpael PERFECT, cf. Isa. 26:3-4)! Trust is crucial in biblical faith.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT

verses.zh: 现在我降旨，无论何方、何国、何族的人，谤讟沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌之　神的，必被凌迟，他的房屋必成粪堆，因为没有别神能这样施行拯救。」
verses.en: I hereby decree[NOTE:1] that any people, nation, or language group that blasphemes[NOTE:2] the God of Shadrach, Meshach, or Abednego will be dismembered and his home reduced to rubble! For there exists no other god who can deliver in this way.”
notes: Aram “from me is placed an edict.”
Aram “speaks negligence.”
verses.commentary:
3:29 "shall be torn limb from limb" This was an ancient form of ANE execution, as was being burned
(cf. Dan. 2:5; 1 Sam. 15:33).

▣ "their houses reduced to a rubbish heap" This was also an ancient form of punishment and
shame (cf. Dan. 2:5; Ezra 6:11).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Why were the Chaldeans of Dan. 3:8 out to get the Hebrew youths?

- Was the image political or religious?

- What are the implications of Dan. 3:17 and 18 for our lives?

- Who was the fourth person in the flames?

verses.zh: 那时王在巴比伦省，高升了沙得拉、米煞、亚伯尼歌。
verses.en: Then Nebuchadnezzar[NOTE:1] promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.
notes: Aram “and the king.” The proper name has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- This chapter shows that the faith of Daniel is equally shared by his three exiled friends. There has been much speculation on
why Daniel was not present that day on the Plains of Dura.

- he was sick

- he was on assignment

- Hippolytus supposed he was watching from a distance (NET Bible, p. 1538, #14)

- the Jewish Study Bible suggests chapter 3 was a separate document that circulated independantly for many years

- This chapter is characterized by

- lists

- the repeating of these lists

- names of government officials (cf. Dan. 3:2,3,27)

- names of musical instruments (cf. Dan. 3:5,7,10,15)

- names of people groups (cf. Dan. 3:4,7; 4:1; 6:25)

- the three Hebrew youths (cf. Dan. 3:12,13,14,16,19,20,22,23,26 [twice],28,29,30)

- The theological issue of God's sovereignty (i.e., Dan. 2:21; see full note there) continues. He is God and He rewards those who trust
(cf. Dan. 3:28) Him.

1Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, the
height of which was sixty cubits and its width six cubits; he set it up on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon. 2Then
Nebuchadnezzar the king sent word to assemble the satraps, the prefects and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the
magistrates and all the rulers of the provinces to come to the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up. 3Then
the satraps, the prefects and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates and all the rulers of the provinces were
assembled for the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up; and they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had
set up. 4Then the herald loudly proclaimed: "To you the command is given, O peoples, nations and men of every language,
5that at the moment you hear the sound of the horn, flute, lyre, trigon, psaltery, bagpipe and all kinds of music, you are to fall down and
worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king has set up. 6But whoever does not fall down and worship shall immediately be
cast into the midst of a furnace of blazing fire." 7Therefore at that time, when all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, flute, lyre, trigon,
psaltery, bagpipe and all kinds of music, all the peoples, nations and men of every language fell down and worshiped the golden image that
Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up.
